identification.name: Aluminum 2024-T3
identification.common_form_notes: The classic aerospace aircraft-skin sheet alloy — high strength-to-weight for its era, though superseded by 7075 where even higher strength is needed. Poor weldability (high copper content, like other 2xxx-series alloys) means it's joined mechanically (rivets, fasteners) rather than welded, unlike 6061.
identification.notes: All mechanical/thermal values are Aluminum Association "Typical" figures from a single MatWeb datasheet — internally consistent (back-calculating shear modulus from the stored E=73.1 GPa and ν=0.33 gives G ≈ 27.5 GPa, matching the source's directly-stated 28.0 GPa closely) and consistent with commonly-cited textbook values for this well-known alloy. Shear strength (283 MPa) is a directly-reported value, not derived. Electrical conductivity (29.6% IACS (International Annealed Copper Standard)) derived from the source's stated electrical resistivity (5.82 µΩ·cm) via %IACS = (1.7241/5.82)×100 — matches the commonly-cited ~30% IACS figure for 2024-T3. Melting point is solidus (502°C); liquidus is 638°C. Strength drops sharply at elevated temperature (source gives 52 MPa UTS (ultimate tensile strength) @ 316°C, 34 MPa @ 371°C) — not recorded as a usable temperature range here since no single service-temperature limit was given, but worth noting this alloy is not a high-temperature choice despite good room-temperature strength. Remains ductile at cryogenic temperatures (18% elongation reported at −196°C). A single fatigue data point (138 MPa @ 5×10⁸ cycles, completely reversed stress, RR Moore machine) is stored as the sole S-N curve point — not a full curve.

typical_usage: Aircraft fuselage skin and structural sheet, truck wheels, structural rivets, and other applications needing high strength-to-weight with good fatigue and fracture resistance. A common comparison point against 6061-T6 (much better weldability/machinability, lower strength) and 7075-T6 (higher strength, worse fatigue/fracture behavior in some regimes).
